title: Earnings Losses of Displaced Workers
research_question: How large and persistent are the earnings losses suffered by high-tenure workers when they lose their jobs, and to what extent do these losses precede separation, vary across industries and local labor markets, and persist even when displaced workers find re-employment in similar firms?
data_description: The authors construct a longitudinal administrative dataset covering a 5 percent sample of Pennsylvania wage and salary workers, built by merging quarterly Unemployment Insurance tax records, UI claims data, and ES202 employer reports. Worker-level quarterly earnings histories span 1974 through 1986 and are linked via Employer Identification Numbers to firm-level information including 4-digit SIC industry, county location, and annual employment levels. Available worker characteristics are limited to year of birth, sex, and firm tenure measured from 1974. The analysis sample comprises prime-age workers born 1930-1959 who had been employed at the same firm since at least 1974, yielding 9,568 separators (with 6+ years of tenure) leaving their firms between 1980 and 1986 and 14,028 continuously employed comparison workers. Separators are split into a 'mass-layoff' subsample (firms whose employment fell more than 30 percent below late-1970s peaks) and a 'nonmass-layoff' subsample.
institutional_context: The setting is the Pennsylvania labor market during the early-to-mid 1980s, a period marked by a severe 1982-83 recession and substantial structural change in U.S. manufacturing. Pennsylvania experienced sharply divergent regional fortunes: the western half, centered on Pittsburgh, suffered double-digit unemployment driven by collapse in primary metals and heavy manufacturing, while the eastern half, including Philadelphia, shared in the growth of the broader Middle Atlantic region. Many large employers undertook substantial workforce reductions or shut down operations, generating a wave of involuntary job losses among long-tenured workers in industries such as steel, motor vehicles, and machinery, alongside more routine separations at firms not undergoing major contractions. This variation in firm-level employment shocks and in local labor market tightness, combined with concerns raised by the 1990-91 recession and debates over trade adjustment and extended unemployment benefits, motivates comparing the earnings trajectories of workers leaving distressed firms with those of otherwise similar workers who remained employed.
